identity.title: Pupils and eye movements: miosis with hypoventilation (opioid), ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus with ataxia (Wernicke), gaze deviation

technique.how: Inspect pupil size and symmetry in ambient then dim light and test light reaction; count respiratory rate for a full minute. Ask the patient to follow a target through the six cardinal positions, watching for horizontal or vertical nystagmus, lateral rectus (VI) palsy, or gaze restriction, and note any sustained conjugate gaze deviation at rest.
technique.prerequisites: Adequate light; patient at least intermittently attentive for pursuit testing.

interpretation.positive_finding: Pinpoint pupils with respirations of 12/min or fewer suggest opioid toxicity and justify naloxone; nystagmus or ophthalmoplegia with ataxia or confusion in an at-risk (alcohol, malnutrition, bariatric) patient meets Caine/EFNS criteria for Wernicke encephalopathy - give IV thiamine before glucose; forced gaze deviation suggests stroke or ongoing seizure.
interpretation.negative_finding: Normal pupils and eye movements do not exclude opioid toxicity (mixed ingestions), Wernicke encephalopathy (most necropsy-proven cases lack the full triad), or nonconvulsive seizure.
interpretation.pitfalls: Miosis also occurs with pontine lesions, cholinergic agents, and organophosphates; hypoxia and mixed overdoses can produce normal or dilated pupils; ocular signs of Wernicke may be subtle (nystagmus only) and are missed without deliberate testing.
interpretation.changes_what: Miosis+bradypnea: naloxone trial and airway support; eye-movement abnormality with ataxia/confusion: empiric IV thiamine; gaze deviation: stroke/seizure pathway (imaging, EEG).

estimates.target_condition: COMPOSITE: classic clinical triad (ocular abnormality + ataxia + confusion) for Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome diagnosed at necropsy
estimates.population: 131 cases of Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome identified at necropsy (retrospective review of hospital clinical records), Sydney, Australia
estimates.quote: only 16% had the classical clinical triad and 19% had no documented clinical signs

sources.citation: Harper CG, Giles M, Finlay-Jones R. Clinical signs in the Wernicke-Korsakoff complex: a retrospective analysis of 131 cases diagnosed at necropsy. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry. 1986;49(4):341-5.

Caine D, Halliday GM, Kril JJ, Harper CG. Operational criteria for the classification of chronic alcoholics: identification of Wernicke's encephalopathy. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry. 1997;62(1):51-60.
Galvin R, Bråthen G, Ivashynka A, Hillbom M, Tanasescu R, Leone MA. EFNS guidelines for diagnosis, therapy and prevention of Wernicke encephalopathy. Eur J Neurol. 2010;17(12):1408-18.
Hoffman JR, Schriger DL, Luo JS. The empiric use of naloxone in patients with altered mental status: a reappraisal. Ann Emerg Med. 1991;20(3):246-52.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not withhold thiamine or naloxone because eye signs are absent when the clinical context is suggestive; do not test eye movements in place of airway management in a hypoventilating patient.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Miosis with respiratory rate <=12 or SpO2 fall needs immediate naloxone and ventilatory support; new gaze deviation with hemiparesis is a stroke alert.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Caine 1997 notes rater variability for specific symptoms although between-rater agreement for diagnostic classification using the criteria was 100% on records (Abstract); no kappa for individual eye signs found.

extraction_notes: Only one numeric estimate was defensible: the classic Wernicke triad had 16% sensitivity among 131 necropsy-proven cases (Harper 1986, Abstract; PMC deposit is abstract-only so per-sign frequencies in the paper's tables could not be verified and are not entered). Entered as COMPOSITE because the triad, not the eye sign alone, is what the abstract quantifies; no controls so no specificity/LR. Caine 1997 (Abstract) reports that the 2-of-4 operational criteria (which include eye signs) had 50% sensitivity when WE co-occurred with hepatic encephalopathy, i.e. criteria-level not sign-level, so not entered as an estimate; full text not open access. EFNS guideline adopts the Caine criteria (Level B). Hoffman 1991 (Abstract) states that respirations <=12 or any of three clinical findings (including miotic pupils) were 'highly sensitive' for naloxone response but reports no numeric sensitivity/specificity for miosis in the abstract, and the search 'opioid overdose[Title] miosis' yielded only a case report; opioid miosis therefore has no entered estimate. No source was found for gaze deviation accuracy within budget.
